2nd edition · 2026 · O'Reilly Media

Designing Data-Intensive Applications

Martin Kleppmann and Chris Riccomini

A first-principles tour of how data systems work — data models, storage engines, encoding, replication, sharding, transactions, the failure modes of distributed systems, consensus, and batch and stream processing — organized around the trade-offs every data system makes, and closing with the ethics of building them.

Start with chapter 1 → SimulationsKey concepts

Each lesson walks the chapter section by section — notes with page references, diagrams, simulations, a recap and a self-check. Use ← → to move between slides.

  • Chapter 6 · pp. 197–250ReplicationReplication keeps a copy of the same data on several machines — for availability, durability, disconnected operation, lower latency, and read scalability.▶ simulation⌘ lab

How the book fits together

The second edition has no part divisions; this grouping is the vault's own reading map, built from the chapters' cross-references.

Threads that cross the groups: storage engines' logs and sorted files (4) return in batch processing (11); replication logs (6) become change data capture (12); consensus and shared logs (10) underpin log-based brokers (12).

Simulations

Interactive models of the mechanisms the book describes. They are embedded in the lessons too; implementations are the vault’s own.

  • Chapter 1Sort the workloadsClassify queries as operational (OLTP) or analytical (OLAP), and datasets as systems of record or derived data — with feedback drawn from the characteristics the book uses.
  • Chapter 2Queueing, overload, and retry stormsPush a server towards its capacity and watch queueing delay explode, then add a load spike with client retries and see it fail to recover.
  • Chapter 2Percentiles and tail latencyExplore why response-time percentiles beat averages, and how fan-out amplifies tail latency.
  • Chapter 3Event sourcing and CQRSRun the book's conference-booking example: commands are validated and become immutable events, materialized views are derived from the log, and a buggy view is fixed by deleting it and replaying the events.
  • Chapter 3Normalize or denormalize?Store a region once and reference it by ID, or copy its name into every profile? Rename a region, read profiles, and watch the costs move between the write path and the read path.
  • Chapter 4B-tree pages, lookups and splitsInsert and look up keys in a small B-tree: follow page references from the root, watch full pages split and the tree grow a level, and crash in the middle of a split with and without a write-ahead log.
  • Chapter 4Column storage and bitmap indexesStore a fact table by column, turn a column into one bitmap per distinct value, run-length encode the bitmaps, and answer IN and AND filters with bitwise OR and AND.
  • Chapter 4Inside an LSM-treeWrite, flush, compact and read from a toy LSM-tree with a write-ahead log and Bloom filters.
  • Chapter 5One record, four encodingsThe book's example record byte by byte in JSON, MessagePack, Protocol Buffers and Avro — hover any byte to see what it encodes and why the sizes are 81, 66, 33 and 32 bytes.
  • Chapter 5Writer’s schema, reader’s schemaChange the book's Avro Person schema — add, remove and rename fields with and without defaults — and see whether old and new code can still read each other's records.
  • Chapter 6Concurrent writes: siblings vs last write winsReplay the book's shopping-cart example: two clients add items concurrently, the server uses version numbers to keep concurrent values as siblings, and last write wins loses items.
  • Chapter 6Replication lag and quorumsWatch replication lag break read-after-write and monotonic reads, lose writes on failover, and see why w + r > n quorums overlap.
  • Chapter 7Local vs global secondary indexesSearch the book's used-car listings by colour and make with local (document-partitioned) and global (term-partitioned) secondary indexes, and count the shards each read and write touches.
  • Chapter 7Sharding and rebalancingCompare hash mod N, a fixed number of shards, and rendezvous hashing when nodes join; see how key-range sharding and hot keys create hot spots.
  • Chapter 8Isolation levels, one interleaving at a timeStep through two interleaved transactions and see which anomalies each isolation level prevents: dirty reads, read skew, lost updates, write skew.
  • Chapter 8Two-phase commit and the in-doubt participantStep a distributed transaction through two-phase commit — prepare, votes, commit point, commit — and inject failures: a no vote, a timeout, a crashed participant, and a coordinator that crashes leaving a participant in doubt.
  • Chapter 9Clock skew and last write winsReplay the book's Figure 9-3: with a few milliseconds of clock skew, last write wins orders a causally later increment before the write it built on and silently drops it. Then measure how many writes are lost as skew grows.
  • Chapter 9Leases, process pauses, and fencing tokensA lease-holder pauses, its lease expires, another client takes over — and the paused client wakes up and writes anyway. Turn on fencing tokens and watch the storage reject it.
  • Chapter 9How long before a node is dead?Choose a timeout for declaring a node dead: watch heartbeat delays vary with network queueing and process pauses, and trade false suspicions against slow detection of a real crash.
  • Chapter 10Consensus: elect a leader, replicate a logA five-node, Raft-style cluster: elect leaders with epoch (term) numbers, replicate log entries to a quorum, crash nodes and partition the network.
  • Chapter 10Ordering events: wall clocks, Lamport clocks, vector clocksPost and reply in the book's three-person chat and compare three ways to order the messages: skewed wall-clock timestamps, Lamport timestamps, and vector clocks that reveal which messages were concurrent.
  • Chapter 11Shuffle and sort-merge joinStep a batch join through map, shuffle, sort and reduce: activity events meet user records by user ID, and a secondary sort keeps reducer memory to one record.
  • Chapter 12Partitioned logs and consumer offsetsProduce keyed messages into a sharded log, consume them with a consumer group that records offsets, then crash a consumer to see messages processed twice, or let one fall behind retention and miss messages.
  • Chapter 12Event time, processing time, and stragglersCount events in tumbling windows by event time and by processing time, decide when to close a window, and handle straggler events.
  • Chapter 12Tumbling, hopping, sliding and session windowsGroup the same stream of user events into tumbling, hopping, sliding and session windows, and see which events each window counts.
  • Chapter 13Dual writes vs a change logTwo clients update the same item at almost the same time. With dual writes, the database and the search index can apply the updates in different orders and stay inconsistent forever; deriving the index from the database's change log cannot.
  • Chapter 13Exactly once, end to endTransfer $11 over a flaky network: responses get lost, the client retries, and money moves twice — unless a request ID travels from the client to a uniqueness constraint in the database.
  • Chapter 14A credit-score feedback loopGive 300 workers random misfortunes, let employers screen applicants by credit score, and watch a temporary setback turn into a self-reinforcing spiral of joblessness.

Key concepts

Ideas that recur across chapters, with the chapters that discuss them. Definitions are the vault's summaries of the book's explanations.

ConceptDefinitionChapters
ACIDThe four safety guarantees traditionally promised by database transactions — atomicity, consistency, isolation, durability — whose actual meanings are narrower and more uneven than the acronym suggests.8 · 13
B-treeA balanced tree of fixed-size pages, overwritten in place, that keeps keys sorted and finds any key in O(log n) page reads — the standard index of relational databases.4 · 8
Change data captureObserving every write committed to a database and publishing it, in commit order, as a stream that other systems consume to keep derived copies in sync.6 · 12 · 13
Column-oriented storageStoring all values of each column together, instead of all values of each row together, so analytical queries read only the columns they need and data compresses far better.4 · 11
Conflict resolutionDetecting when replicas accepted concurrent writes to the same data, and merging them so that all replicas converge to the same state.6 · 9 · 10
ConsensusGetting a group of nodes to agree irrevocably on a value — or on a sequence of values (a shared log) — despite crashes and network problems, as long as a majority is working.7 · 10 · 12 · 13
Derived dataData that is produced by transforming data held elsewhere — and can therefore be recomputed from it — as opposed to a system of record, which holds the authoritative version of each fact.1 · 2 · 3 · 4 · 11 · 12 · 13 · 14
Event sourcingStoring every change to application state as an immutable event in an append-only log, which becomes the source of truth; read-optimized views are derived from it (CQRS).3 · 12 · 13 · 14
Event time and windowsGrouping stream events into time windows by when they happened (event time) rather than when they were processed — and deciding what to do about events that arrive after their window was considered complete.9 · 12 · 13
Fencing tokenA number, increasing with every grant of a lock or lease, that clients must present to the protected resource — which rejects any request carrying a lower number than it has already seen.9 · 10
IdempotenceAn operation is idempotent if performing it several times has the same effect as performing it once — which makes retries safe and turns at-least-once delivery into exactly-once effects.5 · 8 · 11 · 12 · 13
Isolation levelsThe degree to which a database protects concurrent transactions from each other, defined by which race conditions (anomalies) it allows.8 · 10
Leader-based replicationOne replica (the leader) accepts all writes and streams them, in order, to followers that apply the same changes; reads may be served by any replica.6 · 10
LinearizabilityA consistency guarantee under which a replicated object behaves as if there were a single copy and every operation took effect atomically at some instant between its start and its end.6 · 10 · 13
Log-based message brokerA message broker that stores each stream as an append-only, sharded log retained on disk; consumers read sequentially and track their own position (offset) instead of acknowledging and deleting individual messages.5 · 10 · 12 · 13
Logical clocksAlgorithms that assign timestamps by counting events rather than measuring time, so that timestamp order is consistent with causality even when physical clocks disagree.6 · 9 · 10
LSM-treeA log-structured storage engine that buffers writes in a sorted in-memory table, flushes them as immutable sorted files (SSTables), and merges those files in the background.4 · 11
OLTP vs OLAPTwo families of data workload: online transaction processing (many small, low-latency reads and writes of individual records) and online analytical processing (queries that scan and aggregate large numbers of records).1 · 3 · 4 · 11
Partial failureIn a distributed system, some components can fail while others keep working — and a node often cannot tell which, because a missing response is ambiguous.1 · 2 · 9
QuorumA minimum number of nodes that must take part in an operation for it to count — chosen so that any two quorums overlap, which lets the system decide safely even when some nodes are unreachable.6 · 9 · 10
Replication lagThe delay between a write on the leader and its application on a follower; reads from lagging replicas produce anomalies that specific consistency guarantees rule out.6 · 10 · 13
Response-time percentilesDescribing latency as a distribution — median (p50), p95, p99, p999 — rather than an average, because users experience individual requests and the slowest ones matter most.2 · 7
Schema evolutionChanging the structure of data over time while old and new code continue to read each other's data: backward compatibility (new code reads old data) and forward compatibility (old code reads new data).3 · 5
ShardingSplitting a dataset into subsets (shards, partitions) stored on different nodes, so data volume and load can grow beyond one machine.2 · 7 · 13
ShuffleThe distributed sort at the heart of batch processing: every record is routed by key to the task responsible for that key, so all records with the same key end up together, in sorted order.4 · 11
Two-phase commitA protocol for committing a transaction atomically across several nodes: a coordinator asks every participant to prepare, and only if all promise to commit does it record and broadcast the decision to commit.8 · 10 · 13
Write skewA race in which two transactions read the same data, each makes a decision based on what it read, and each writes a different object — so neither write conflicts with the other, yet together they violate an invariant.6 · 8 · 13

Notes restate the book with printed page references; anything else is labelled as the vault’s own. Source and fidelity notes: README.md.
